newsitem.title: CHINA: China parliament to mull criminal law amendments.
newsitem.headline: China parliament to mull criminal law amendments.

text.p: China's parliament will consider scrapping the crime of "counter-revolution" and other amendments to the criminal law during its annual session starting at the weekend, a parliamentary spokesman said on Friday.

Drafted changes to the 17-year-old criminal code would include reclassifying counter-revolutionary crimes as threats to state security, boosting anti-graft legislation and curbing abuses by law enforcers, National People's Congress spokesman Zhou Jue said.

"The amendment of the criminal law is a major event in our efforts to improve our criminal legal system and judicial system and is also of major significance for us to further achieve the objective of running the country according to law," Zhou said.

The amendments would not change the basis of the criminal law, but would clarify the principles of legally determining crimes and penalties, with penalties being decided according to the crime committed and equality before the law, he said.

The changes were needed to cope with the spread of such crimes as corruption and smuggling and the rise of new kinds of lawbreaking such as computer crime, money laundering and value-added tax fraud, he said.
He gave no details of the replacement of crimes of "counter-revolution" with the offence of jeopardising state security, a move seen as step away from China's radical past.

The crime of counter-revolution has for decades been used as a catch-all, punishing anyone whose opinions were judged hostile to the state, and some analysts say the new offences were likely to be used in the same way.

Zhou said the criminal law amendments would also include more detailed descriptions of crimes and penalties and would help curb abuses by law enforcers, who often enjoy wide discretionary powers under the existing code.

China has long been been criticised by human rights activists for inadequate controls on police and for tolerating the widespread abuse of suspects, but officials say they have made great strides in bringing order to criminal justice.

The last annual session of the Eighth National People's Congress, which begins on Saturday, is also scheduled to consider a draft defence law and proposals for the selection of deputies from Hong Kong.
The parliament is widely considered a rubber-stamp body but has in recent years displayed occasional flashes of independence by showing disagreement over some government appointments or draft laws.
